title: Why does an application report "connection pool exhausted" while the database sits mostly idle (connections held by long/idle-in-transaction sessions, often an external call made inside a transaction), and how does `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` help?
shortTitle: Why does an app report "connection pool exhausted" while the database sits mostly idle?

s1_definition.profdef: Pool exhaustion with an idle database happens when borrowed connections are held open but not doing database work, so the pool empties while the database has nothing to execute. The classic cause is a connection kept inside an open transaction while the thread waits on something slow and unrelated, most often an external HTTP call made inside a `@Transactional` method. PostgreSQL shows these as `idle in transaction`, and the setting `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` automatically aborts a transaction that sits idle too long, releasing the connection and surfacing the bug.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India has three ledger phone lines. A teller picks up a line to start recording Rajesh's loan, but mid-way they put the ledger clerk on hold and walk off to phone an outside credit bureau that takes thirty seconds to answer. The ledger clerk sits there idle, the line is tied up, and soon all three lines are held by tellers waiting on outside calls. Customers queue and get "all lines busy," yet the ledger room is silent because no actual recording is happening. The fix is a rule that says any line held with the clerk on hold for more than a few seconds is force-released.
s1_definition.oneliner: The pool empties because connections are held inside open transactions waiting on slow non-database work; `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` kills those stuck transactions and frees the connections.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Pool exhaustion with an idle database happens when borrowed connections are held open but not doing database work, so the pool empties while the database has nothing to execute. The classic cause is a connection kept inside an open transaction while the thread waits on something slow and unrelated, most often an external HTTP call made inside a `@Transactional` method. PostgreSQL shows these as `idle in transaction`, and the setting `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` automatically aborts a transaction that sits idle too long, releasing the connection and surfacing the bug.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India has three ledger phone lines. A teller picks up a line to start recording Rajesh's loan, but mid-way they put the ledger clerk on hold and walk off to phone an outside credit bureau that takes thirty seconds to answer. The ledger clerk sits there idle, the line is tied up, and soon all three lines are held by tellers waiting on outside calls. Customers queue and get "all lines busy," yet the ledger room is silent because no actual recording is happening. The fix is a rule that says any line held with the clerk on hold for more than a few seconds is force-released.

**One line to remember:** The pool empties because connections are held inside open transactions waiting on slow non-database work; `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` kills those stuck transactions and frees the connections.

sections.s2_technical:
A pool connection is "in use" from the moment you borrow it until you return it, regardless of whether the database is actually executing a query. So a connection can be fully idle from the database's point of view while still counted as borrowed by the pool. If enough connections are in that state, the pool reports exhaustion even though the database CPU and disk are near zero. This is the tell-tale signature: application errors about pool timeouts, but a calm database.

The most common root cause is doing slow, non-database work inside a transaction. A method annotated `@Transactional` opens a transaction on a pooled connection at the start and holds it until the method returns. If that method makes an external HTTP call — say to a credit bureau, a payment gateway, or another microservice — the connection is pinned for the entire duration of that call, which might be seconds, while the database does nothing. Under load, every request pins a connection for the external call's duration, the pool drains, and new requests block and time out waiting to borrow. Other causes are long-running reports holding a connection, forgetting to close a connection so it leaks, or a transaction left open due to a missing commit or rollback on an error path.

PostgreSQL exposes these sessions in `pg_stat_activity` with state `idle in transaction`, which is the diagnostic. The setting `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` tells PostgreSQL to automatically abort any transaction that has been idle for longer than the timeout, rolling it back and freeing the server side. This does two good things: it prevents a stuck transaction from holding locks and bloating the database indefinitely, and it converts a silent hang into a loud error that points at the offending code. It is a safety net, not a cure. The real fix is architectural: never make external calls inside a transaction. You restructure the code so the transaction does only the database work and commits quickly, and the slow external call happens before or after the transaction, outside its boundary. A senior nuance is to also set a statement timeout and a pool leak-detection threshold so you catch both slow queries and leaked connections, and to keep transactions as short as physically possible.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the loan-approval service was timing out with "connection pool exhausted" during busy hours, yet the database dashboards showed almost no activity. Investigation showed the service called an external credit-bureau API inside a `@Transactional` method, so each request held a connection for the two-to-three-second bureau call while doing no database work. This is exactly the idle-in-transaction exhaustion pattern.

Problem 2 — The fix was to move the external call outside the transaction so the transaction only touches the database and commits in milliseconds, and to set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` as a safety net so any future offender is aborted and logged loudly. This is exactly the correct remedy.

The mini-project shows the broken version where the bureau call sits inside the transaction and the fixed version where the bureau call happens first and the transaction is short, with comments explaining how `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` protects the database.

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  datasource:
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 10
      connection-timeout: 3000
      leak-detection-threshold: 20000   # warn if a connection is held > 20s
  jpa:
    properties:
      hibernate.connection.provider_disables_autocommit: true
# On PostgreSQL set the server-side safety net:
#   idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '10s'
#   statement_timeout = '5s'
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build and run
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/idle-in-transaction-demo-1.0.0.jar

# Diagnose idle-in-transaction sessions live
psql -d bankdb -c "SELECT pid, state, now()-xact_start AS txn_age, query
  FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'idle in transaction' ORDER BY txn_age DESC;"

# Apply the safety net
psql -d bankdb -c "ALTER SYSTEM SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '10s'; SELECT pg_reload_conf();"
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: a burst of loan-approval requests against a pool of ten, first using the bad service, then the good one.

Step 1 (bad): A request enters `approve`. Spring opens a transaction on a pooled connection at the method start. The pool now shows one fewer available.

Step 2 (bad): The method calls the credit bureau, which takes 2.5 seconds. For that whole time the connection is borrowed and inside an open transaction, but the database executes nothing — it is idle in transaction.

Step 3 (bad): With more than ten concurrent requests, all ten connections are pinned by bureau calls. The eleventh request blocks trying to borrow and times out after three seconds with "connection pool exhausted," even though the database CPU is near zero.

Step 4 (good): A request enters the good `approve`. The bureau call runs first with no connection borrowed. Only after the score returns does `persist` borrow a connection, run a quick update, commit in milliseconds, and return the connection.

Step 5 (good): Because connections are held only for the fast update, ten connections serve a high request rate comfortably, and the pool never exhausts.

```text
# BAD
09:55:01 WARN  HikariPool - bank-pool - Connection not available, request timed out after 3000ms
# pg_stat_activity: 10 sessions state='idle in transaction'  (DB idle!)

# GOOD
09:56:10 INFO  GoodLoanService - Loan LN-88 approved with score 760 (short txn)
# pg_stat_activity: sessions state='idle' (returned), pool healthy
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  ── BAD: external call inside transaction ──
  request → @Transactional approve()
     │ BEGIN  (borrow connection)
     │ bureau.fetchScore()  ←─ 2.5s, DB IDLE IN TRANSACTION, connection pinned
     │ UPDATE loan          (finally some DB work)
     │ COMMIT (return connection)
     ▼
  under load: all 10 connections pinned by bureau calls → POOL EXHAUSTED
             (DB CPU ≈ 0%)

  ── GOOD: external call outside transaction ──
  request → approve()
     │ bureau.fetchScore()  ←─ 2.5s, NO connection held
     ▼
     persist()  @Transactional
        │ BEGIN (borrow) → UPDATE loan → COMMIT (return)   ~5ms
     ▼
  pool stays healthy; idle_in_transaction_session_timeout=10s as safety net
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The paradox of a pool reporting exhaustion while the database sits idle is explained by one fact: a pooled connection counts as in use from the moment you borrow it until you return it, whether or not the database is actually executing anything. So if connections are held open but doing no database work, the pool drains while the database CPU stays near zero. That signature — pool timeout errors with a calm database — points almost always at one root cause: slow, non-database work being done inside an open transaction.

The classic offender is an external HTTP call made inside a `@Transactional` method. Spring opens a transaction on a pooled connection at the start of the method and holds it until the method returns, so if the method calls a credit bureau, a payment gateway, or another service that takes a couple of seconds, the connection is pinned for that whole time while the database does nothing. Under load every request pins a connection for the external call, the pool empties, and new requests block and time out. PostgreSQL shows these as `idle in transaction` in `pg_stat_activity`, which is the diagnostic.

The setting `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` is the safety net: it tells PostgreSQL to automatically abort any transaction that has been idle beyond the timeout, which frees the server side, releases locks, and turns a silent hang into a loud error that points at the bug. But it is a safety net, not a cure. The real fix is architectural — never make an external call inside a transaction; restructure so the slow call happens outside the transaction boundary and the transaction does only the database work and commits in milliseconds. At the National Bank of India our loan service was exhausting its pool exactly this way because the bureau call sat inside the transaction; we moved the call outside, kept the transaction tiny, and set an idle-in-transaction timeout and a statement timeout as safety nets. The line I always state is that the pool empties because connections are held inside open transactions waiting on slow non-database work, and the timeout frees them while the proper fix is to keep transactions short and database-only.

---

keyPoints: Connection pool: reuse DB connections — avoid create/destroy overhead
HikariCP: fastest Java connection pool (Spring Boot default)
Pool size: too small = thread waiting, too large = DB overloaded
